subject: religious-studies
title: The Moral Argument and Religious Experience
welcome_lead: Carry a lantern into the territory of conscience and encounter, where Kant and James seek God in the moral and mystical life.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on moral arguments and arguments from religious experience.
final_note: Conscience and encounter are stubborn data that secular theories must still account for.

concepts.def: From the Critique of Practical Reason (1788): God's existence is a postulate of practical reason, securing the proportion of virtue and happiness in the summum bonum.
John Henry Newman's view that the voice of conscience points to a personal lawgiver: God.
The 'highest good': perfect virtue united with proportionate happiness; for Kant, attainable only if God and immortality exist.
American philosopher whose Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) classified mystical experience as ineffable, noetic, transient, and passive.
Rudolf Otto's term in The Idea of the Holy (1917) for the non-rational experience of the holy as 'mysterium tremendum et fascinans'.
Swinburne's principle that, in the absence of defeaters, things are probably as they seem; applied to religious experience.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), Kant argues that the moral law commands us to pursue the highest good: a world in which perfect virtue is matched by proportionate happiness.

Since we cannot guarantee this proportion ourselves, we must postulate God as the moral guarantor and immortality as the arena in which the highest good is realised. God is not proved theoretically but presupposed practically.

William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), studies mystical states empirically. He identifies four marks: ineffability (resistance to description), noetic quality (revelatory of truth), transiency, and passivity.

James defends the cognitive significance of such experiences pragmatically: by their fruits we shall know them.

Rudolf Otto's The Idea of the Holy (1917) coined the term 'numinous' to name a unique category of religious experience.

The numinous combines mysterium tremendum (awe before the wholly other) with fascinans (irresistible attraction). It is non-rational and yet, Otto insists, an irreducible datum of the religious life.
